claim: Schizophrenia results in part from a failure of prefrontal networks.
source: Schizophrenia results in part from a failure of prefrontal networks but we lack full understanding of how disruptions at a synaptic level cause failures at the network level.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the research problem, drawing on established knowledge about schizophrenia and prefrontal cortex dysfunction.

claim: There is a lack of full understanding of how disruptions at a synaptic level cause failures at the network level in schizophrenia.
source: Schizophrenia results in part from a failure of prefrontal networks but we lack full understanding of how disruptions at a synaptic level cause failures at the network level.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific understanding, which is the motivation for the study.

claim: The authors developed a recurrent spiking network model of prefrontal local circuits.
source: To address that question, we developed a recurrent spiking network model of prefrontal local circuits that can explain the link between NMDAR synaptic and 0-lag spike synchrony deficits we recently observed in a pharmacological monkey model of prefrontal network failure in schizophrenia.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used in the study.

claim: The network model can explain the link between NMDAR synaptic and 0-lag spike synchrony deficits observed in a pharmacological monkey model of prefrontal network failure in schizophrenia.
source: To address that question, we developed a recurrent spiking network model of prefrontal local circuits that can explain the link between NMDAR synaptic and 0-lag spike synchrony deficits we recently observed in a pharmacological monkey model of prefrontal network failure in schizophrenia.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results presented in the manuscript, which demonstrate the model's ability to reproduce experimental observations.

claim: Reducing recurrent NMDAR synaptic currents prevents the network from shifting from a steady to oscillatory state in response to extrinsic inputs.
source: We show that reducing recurrent NMDAR synaptic currents prevents the network from shifting from a steady to oscillatory state in response to extrinsic inputs such as might occur during behavior.
evidence: This is a key finding from the network simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dynamic modulation of 0-lag spike synchrony was observed between neurons in monkey prefrontal cortex during behavior.
source: These findings strongly parallel dynamic modulation of 0-lag spike synchrony we observed between neurons in monkey prefrontal cortex during behavior, as well as the suppression of this 0-lag spiking by administration of NMDAR antagonists.
evidence: This refers to previously published experimental data from the authors' group.

claim: Administration of NMDAR antagonists suppresses 0-lag spiking in monkey prefrontal cortex.
source: These findings strongly parallel dynamic modulation of 0-lag spike synchrony we observed between neurons in monkey prefrontal cortex during behavior, as well as the suppression of this 0-lag spiking by administration of NMDAR antagonists.
evidence: This refers to previously published experimental data from the authors' group.

claim: NMDAR synaptic malfunction has been implicated as causal in schizophrenia.
source: NMDAR synaptic malfunction has been implicated as causal in schizophrenia (Fromer et al., 2014; Schizophrenia Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2014; Timms et al., 2013), and loss of NMDAR synaptic function in prefrontal networks is believed to contribute to cognitive deficits as well as clinical symptoms in the disease (Goldman-Rakic, 1999; Javitt et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Loss of NMDAR synaptic function in prefrontal networks is believed to contribute to cognitive deficits and clinical symptoms in schizophrenia.
source: NMDAR synaptic malfunction has been implicated as causal in schizophrenia (Fromer et al., 2014; Schizophrenia Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2014; Timms et al., 2013), and loss of NMDAR synaptic function in prefrontal networks is believed to contribute to cognitive deficits as well as clinical symptoms in the disease (Goldman-Rakic, 1999; Javitt et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Blocking NMDAR altered neural dynamics in prefrontal cortex of monkeys performing a cognitive control task.
source: To address these questions, we recently investigated how blocking NMDAR altered neural dynamics and effective communication between neurons in prefrontal cortex of monkeys performing a cognitive control task measuring deficits in schizophrenia (Blackman et al., 2013; Jones et al., 2010; Kummerfeld et al., 2020; Zick et al., 2018).
evidence: This refers to previously published experimental work by the authors.

claim: Reducing NMDAR synaptic communication reduced the frequency of synchronous ('0-lag') spiking between neurons.
source: We found that reducing NMDAR synaptic communication reduced the frequency of synchronous ('0-lag') spiking between neurons, as well as effective communication between neurons on timescales consistent with monosynaptic interactions between them (Kummerfeld et al., 2020; Zick et al., 2022; Zick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from previously published experimental work by the authors.

claim: Reducing NMDAR synaptic communication reduced effective communication between neurons on timescales consistent with monosynaptic interactions.
source: We found that reducing NMDAR synaptic communication reduced the frequency of synchronous ('0-lag') spiking between neurons, as well as effective communication between neurons on timescales consistent with monosynaptic interactions between them (Kummerfeld et al., 2020; Zick et al., 2022; Zick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from previously published experimental work by the authors.

claim: The network is comprised of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons embedded in a sparsely connected recurrent network employing realistic NMDAR, GABAR, and AMPAR mediated synaptic currents.
source: The network is comprised of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons embedded in a sparsely connected recurrent network employing realistic NMDAR, GABAR, and AMPAR mediated synaptic currents.
evidence: This describes the structure of the computational model developed in the study.

claim: Synchrony can occur naturally in cortical neurons due to local recurrent network connectivity, even when external afferent inputs are entirely uncorrelated.
source: For cortical neurons synchrony can occur naturally due to the local recurrent network connectivity, even when external afferent inputs are entirely uncorrelated.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement based on prior modeling studies.

claim: Synchrony can arise in randomly connected recurrent networks operating in asynchronous irregular and synchronous irregular regimes.
source: Theoretical studies have shown that such synchrony can arise in randomly connected recurrent networks operating in asynchronous irregular (Amit, 1989; Amit and Brunel, 1997; Brunel, 2000; Renart et al., 2010; van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996; Vicente et al., 2008) and synchronous irregular regimes (Brunel, 2000; Brunel and Hakim, 1999; Brunel and Wang, 2003; Ledoux and Brunel, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: In asynchronous irregular regime, individual neurons fire spikes highly irregularly at low rates and population spike rate is steady in time.
source: In both regimes, individual neurons fire spikes highly irregularly at low rates, a typical situation in a cortex. The major distinction is that in an asynchronous regime population spike rate is steady in time, whereas in a synchronous regime it becomes oscillatory.
evidence: This describes characteristics of the asynchronous irregular regime based on theoretical understanding.

claim: In synchronous irregular regime, individual neurons fire spikes highly irregularly at low rates and population spike rate becomes oscillatory.
source: In both regimes, individual neurons fire spikes highly irregularly at low rates, a typical situation in a cortex. The major distinction is that in an asynchronous regime population spike rate is steady in time, whereas in a synchronous regime it becomes oscillatory.
evidence: This describes characteristics of the synchronous irregular regime based on theoretical understanding.

claim: Simulated prefrontal networks operating near the boundary between steady and oscillatory regimes achieve biologically realistic stochastic spike trains and firing rates of excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: First, such networks achieve biologically realistic stochastic spike trains and firing rates of excitatory and inhibitory neurons in prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This is a finding from the network simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Increased extrinsic inputs shift networks from a steady to an oscillatory regime causing emergence of 0-lag spiking between neurons.
source: Second, increased extrinsic inputs, such as those that might occur during behavior, shift these networks from a steady to an oscillatory regime that causes the emergence of 0-lag spiking between neurons as they stochastically entrain to oscillatory population activity.
evidence: This is a finding from the network simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reducing recurrent NMDAR synaptic currents prevents networks from transitioning into oscillatory activity in response to extrinsic inputs.
source: Third, and perhaps most importantly, we show that reducing recurrent NMDAR synaptic currents prevents these networks from transitioning into oscillatory activity in response to extrinsic inputs, thereby preventing the emergence of 0-lag spike synchrony.
evidence: This is a key finding from the network simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Prior modeling studies have not accounted for the range of experimental observations addressed in the current study.
source: Although prior modeling studies have addressed the relationship between NMDAR function and oscillatory activity in prefrontal networks (Brunel and Wang, 2003; Compte et al., 2000; Kirli et al., 2014; Wang, 1999), none account for this range of experimental observations.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the novelty of the current work relative to prior studies.

claim: Spike synchrony remained relatively weak and unchanged during the cue and delay periods in both drug-naive and drug conditions.
source: Figure 1A shows that spike synchrony obtained from trials aligned to the cue onset (time 0) remained relatively weak and unchanged during the cue and delay periods, until the probe onset, in both drug-naive and drug conditions.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Synchrony started to increase sharply about 200ms before the motor response in the drug-naive condition and reached its peak at the time of the response.
source: It is seen that synchrony started to increase sharply about 200ms before the motor response in the drug-naive condition and reached its peak at the time of the response (Figure 1B, black).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Spike rate started to increase before the response but more gradually and starting earlier before the response in the drug-naive condition.
source: The spike rate also started to increase before the response but more gradually and starting earlier before the response (Figure 1D, black).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both spike synchrony and spike rate exhibited secondary peaks occurring approximately 150–250ms after the response.
source: Both spike synchrony (Figure 1B) and spike rate (Figure 1D) exhibited secondary peaks occurring approximately 150–250ms after the response.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1D.

claim: In the drug condition, the increase in spike synchrony at the time of the response was markedly weakened.
source: In the drug condition, however, the increase in spike synchrony at the time of the response was markedly weakened (Figure 1B, magenta).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the drug condition, the increase in spike rate was reduced, although less dramatically than synchrony.
source: The increase in spike rate was also reduced, although less dramatically (Figure 1D, magenta).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: NMDAR blockage induces desynchronization of spiking activity.
source: We term this effect as NMDAR blockage induced desynchronization of spiking activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The network comprises excitatory and inhibitory neurons representing populations of pyramidal cells and interneurons.
source: The network comprises excitatory and inhibitory neurons representing populations of pyramidal cells and interneurons, respectively.
evidence: This describes the structure of the computational model.

claim: All neurons are modeled as leaky integrate-and-fire units.
source: All neurons are modeled as leaky integrate-and-fire units (see, e.g., Dayan and Abbott, 2001).
evidence: This describes the neuron model used in the simulations.

claim: Synaptic connections are random and sparse, but the number of connections received by individual neurons is large.
source: Synaptic connections are random and sparse, but the number of connections received by individual neurons is large.
evidence: This describes the connectivity structure of the model network.

claim: Each neuron receives external connections from excitatory neurons outside of the network that fire spikes with rate νX.
source: In addition to the recurrent local connections, each neuron also receives external connections from excitatory neurons outside of the network that fire spikes with rate νX.
evidence: This describes the external input to the model network.

claim: Recurrent synaptic currents of excitatory connections are two-component, mediated by AMPA and NMDA receptors.
source: Recurrent synaptic currents of excitatory connections are two-component, mediated by AMPA and NMDA receptors, whereas currents of inhibitory connections are mediated by GABAA receptors (GABA thereafter).
evidence: This describes the synaptic mechanisms in the model.

claim: Currents of inhibitory connections are mediated by GABAA receptors.
source: Recurrent synaptic currents of excitatory connections are two-component, mediated by AMPA and NMDA receptors, whereas currents of inhibitory connections are mediated by GABAA receptors (GABA thereafter).
evidence: This describes the synaptic mechanisms in the model.

claim: External currents represent noisy inputs due to background synaptic activity and are mediated by AMPA receptors.
source: External currents represent the noisy inputs due to the background synaptic activity and are mediated by AMPA receptors.
evidence: This describes the external input currents in the model.

claim: The model entails eight maximal synaptic conductance parameters.
source: Thus, the model entails eight maximal synaptic conductance parameters gX,α, gAMPA,α, gNMDA,α, gGABA,α corresponding to the external AMPA, recurrent AMPA, NMDA, and GABA currents (α=E,I for excitatory and inhibitory neurons, respectively).
evidence: This describes the parameters of the model.

claim: Mean field analysis is used to derive synaptic conductance parameters providing desired firing rates.
source: To produce a desired regime of network dynamics (asynchronous or synchronous) with a given firing rate of excitatory and inhibitory neurons νE and νI, respectively, the values of the conductance parameters should be properly adjusted. For this purpose, we used mean field analysis.
evidence: This describes the analytical method used in the study.

claim: Population mean firing rates in the asynchronous stationary state can be parametrized by three parameters expressed as ratios of component synaptic currents.
source: In this framework, population mean firing rates vE0 and vI0 in the asynchronous stationary state of the network can be effectively parametrized by three parameters expressed as ratios of component synaptic currents: IAMPA/IGABA, INMDA/IGABA, and IX,E/Iθ,E, where IR is the mean current of the R-receptor mediated synapse (R=X,AMPA,NMDA,GABA), and Iθ,E is the current that is needed for an excitatory neuron to reach firing threshold θ in absence of recurrent feedback.
evidence: This describes the parametrization used in the mean field analysis.

claim: Linear stability analysis is conducted to understand if the network develops oscillatory instability.
source: While the mean field analysis allows us to determine synaptic conductances that achieve desired firing rates of neurons, whether these rates remain stable over time is another issue. To address it, we conduct a linear stability analysis of the asynchronous state to understand if the network develops oscillatory instability caused by small fluctuations in population firing rates.
evidence: This describes the analytical method used to assess network stability.

claim: The asynchronous state is stable when λ<0.
source: The asynchronous state is stable when λ<0; in this case small perturbations of firing rates cause exponentially damped oscillation of network activity.
evidence: This describes the stability criterion for the asynchronous state.

claim: The case λ=0 corresponds to the onset of instability of the asynchronous state and the emergence of sustained sinusoidal oscillations.
source: The case λ=0 corresponds to the onset of instability of the asynchronous state and the emergence of sustained sinusoidal oscillations of population average firing rates with frequency ω; in the oscillatory regime spike trains remain sparse and irregular but at each oscillation cycle a random subset of network neurons fire synchronously giving rise to the synchronous irregular state.
evidence: This describes the critical boundary between asynchronous and synchronous states.

claim: When λ>0, small fluctuations develop oscillatory instability with exponentially growing amplitude.
source: Lastly, when λ>0, small fluctuations in the stationary rates develop oscillatory instability with the amplitude of oscillations growing exponentially in time; however, higher order terms neglected in linear analysis can eventually saturate the instability growth (Brunel and Hakim, 1999), resulting in a stable oscillation with a finite amplitude.
evidence: This describes the unstable oscillatory regime.

claim: The balance between AMPA and GABA currents controls the network frequency at the onset of oscillation.
source: In the circuit model, the balance between the AMPA component of recurrent excitation and GABA inhibition controls the network frequency at the onset of oscillation, consistent with results in Brunel and Wang, 2003.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, consistent with prior work.

claim: Network frequency at the onset of oscillation is virtually independent of the balance between NMDA and GABA currents.
source: This frequency is virtually independent of the balance between the tonic component of recurrent excitation mediated by the NMDAR and GABA inhibition.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: The balance between NMDA and GABA currents determines the strength of modulation of external synaptic input needed for switching between asynchronous and synchronous states.
source: However, the balance between the NMDA and GABA currents determines the strength of modulation of the external synaptic input needed for switching between the asynchronous stationary and synchronous oscillatory states in the absence and presence of NMDAR antagonist.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: The oscillatory instability growth rate λ directly depends on AMPAR synaptic conductance.
source: We showed that λ, in essence, directly depends only on the AMPAR synaptic conductance; it is virtually independent of the NMDAR conductance due to the slow synaptic decay time constant, while the dependence on the GABAR conductance is much weaker compared to AMPAR because of nearly 90° effective phase lag introduced by synaptic filtering.
evidence: This is a finding from the analytical approximation of the instability growth rate.

claim: The oscillatory instability growth rate λ is virtually independent of NMDAR conductance due to slow synaptic decay time constant.
source: We showed that λ, in essence, directly depends only on the AMPAR synaptic conductance; it is virtually independent of the NMDAR conductance due to the slow synaptic decay time constant, while the dependence on the GABAR conductance is much weaker compared to AMPAR because of nearly 90° effective phase lag introduced by synaptic filtering.
evidence: This is a finding from the analytical approximation of the instability growth rate.

claim: The dependence of λ on GABAR conductance is much weaker compared to AMPAR because of nearly 90° effective phase lag introduced by synaptic filtering.
source: We showed that λ, in essence, directly depends only on the AMPAR synaptic conductance; it is virtually independent of the NMDAR conductance due to the slow synaptic decay time constant, while the dependence on the GABAR conductance is much weaker compared to AMPAR because of nearly 90° effective phase lag introduced by synaptic filtering.
evidence: This is a finding from the analytical approximation of the instability growth rate.

claim: λ depends on NMDAR, GABAR, and AMPAR conductances and external rate indirectly via their effect on the operating point of the neuron's input current-output frequency response function.
source: However, λ depends on the NMDAR, GABAR as well as AMPAR conductances and external rate indirectly via their effect on the operating point of the neuron's input current-output frequency response function.
evidence: This is a finding from the analytical approximation of the instability growth rate.

claim: The direct dependence manifests the essential influence of AMPAR synaptic conductance on the strength of an excitatory-inhibitory feedback loop.
source: The direct dependence manifests the essential influence of the AMPAR synaptic conductance on the strength of an excitatory-inhibitory feedback loop via fast excitatory to excitatory and excitatory to inhibitory recurrent connections.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the analytical results.

claim: The indirect dependence manifests the influence of synaptic conductances and external rate on the location of the operating point on the current-frequency response curve.
source: The indirect dependence manifests the influence of the synaptic conductances and external rate on the location of the operating point on the current-frequency response curve and, therefore, the slope of the response function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the analytical results.

claim: The steepness of the slope of the response function determines the amplitude of the neuron's response to dynamically varying input current.
source: The steepness of the slope, in turn, determines the amplitude of the neuron's response to dynamically varying input current and, therefore, affects the strength of excitatory feedback.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the analytical results.

claim: Both AMPAR and NMDAR conductances affect λ indirectly by influencing the amplitude of the neuron's response to varying input current.
source: Both AMPAR and NMDAR conductances affect λ indirectly by influencing the amplitude of the neuron's response to varying input current.
evidence: This is a finding from the analytical approximation.

claim: AMPAR conductance affects λ directly by influencing the strength of fast excitatory feedback, unlike NMDAR.
source: However, because AMPA currents are much faster than NMDA currents, unlike NMDAR, AMPAR conductance also affects λ directly by influencing the strength of fast excitatory feedback.
evidence: This is a finding from the analytical approximation.

claim: Previous work suggested that NMDAR mediated recurrent currents have a stabilizing effect on network activity.
source: Previous work (Wang, 1999) suggested that NMDAR mediated recurrent currents have a stabilizing effect on the network activity.
evidence: This is a reference to prior theoretical work.

claim: Compte et al. (2000) showed that with less NMDA but more AMPA currents, the asynchronous steady state becomes unstable and neurons begin to synchronize.
source: Compte and colleagues (Compte et al., 2000) carried out spiking network simulations with different relative contributions of the NMDAR and AMPAR mediated currents to the recurrent excitation and showed that with less NMDA but more AMPA currents, the asynchronous steady state becomes unstable and neurons begin to synchronize, leading to network oscillations in the gamma band.
evidence: This is a reference to prior modeling work.

claim: In Compte et al. (2000), blocking NMDAR caused desynchronization, whereas in simulations reducing NMDAR currents provoked strong synchronization.
source: At first glance, these simulation results seem to contradict the experimental findings in Zick et al., 2018. Indeed, in the neural recording experiments blocking NMDAR caused desynchronization of neurons, whereas in the simulations (Compte et al., 2000) the reduction of NMDAR currents provoked strong synchronization.
evidence: This is a comparison between prior modeling work and experimental observations.

claim: The current model and theoretical analysis explains the apparent paradox between Compte et al. (2000) simulations and experimental findings.
source: Our model and theoretical analysis allows to explain this apparent paradox.
evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the current work.

claim: The asynchronous state becomes unstable and oscillation emerges when excitatory feedback from fast AMPA currents becomes sufficiently strong and is followed by strong inhibitory feedback from slower GABA currents.
source: In general, the asynchronous state becomes unstable and oscillation emerges when an excitatory feedback from the fast AMPA currents becomes sufficiently strong and is followed by a strong inhibitory feedback from the slower GABA currents (Brunel and Wang, 2003; Compte et al., 2000; Tsodyks et al., 1997; Wang, 1999).
evidence: This is a general principle from prior theoretical work.

claim: In Compte et al. (2000), concurrent increasing AMPAR and decreasing NMDAR conductances nullifies the indirect effect on instability growth rate.
source: In Compte et al., 2000, the concurrent increasing AMPAR and decreasing NMDAR conductances nullifies the indirect effect because contributions from the changes in the NMDAR and AMPAR mediated currents to the average total synaptic current, in essence, cancel each other.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism in prior work based on the current analysis.

claim: In the current model, enhancement of recurrent excitatory feedback is entirely due to the indirect mechanism through external rate increase.
source: In our model, by contrast, there is no direct effect on the instability growth rate because the AMPAR conductance is kept fixed, and the enhancement of recurrent excitatory feedback is entirely due to the indirect mechanism. It is achieved through external rate increase at a certain strength of the NMDAR conductance resulting in the neuron's operating point shift toward a steeper slope above the point of the critical network.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism in the current model.

claim: When NMDAR conductance is set to zero, the same increase in external rate no longer provides strong enough excitatory feedback.
source: However, when the NMDAR conductance is set to zero, the average total synaptic current is reduced, and the operating point moves down to such locus that it cannot be shifted above the point of the critical network by the same increase in external rate. As a result, external rate increase no longer provides a strong enough excitatory feedback, the network remains in asynchronous state, and no increase in synchrony occurs, consistent with observations in Zick et al., 2018 when NMDAR is blocked.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism in the current model.

claim: Prefrontal neurons exhibit persistent activity associated with maintenance of information in working memory.
source: In monkeys performing a memory-guided saccade task, prefrontal neurons exhibit persistent activity that is associated with the maintenance of information in working memory (Chafee and Goldman-Rakic, 1998; Funahashi et al., 1989; Goldman-Rakic, 1995).
evidence: This is a reference to prior experimental work.

claim: Prior theoretical studies investigated how reducing NMDAR function destabilizes attractor states in prefrontal networks during delay periods.
source: Prior theoretical studies have investigated circuit and synaptic mechanisms that can generate persistent activity in recurrent prefrontal networks, specifically addressing how reducing NMDAR function destabilizes attractor states (patterns of stable neural activity) in these networks during a delay period (when the memory of the stimulus must be retained) leading to working memory deficits (Calvin and Redish, 2021; Compte et al., 2000; Funahashi et al., 1989; Goldman‐Rakic, 1987; Loh et al., 2007; Murray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a reference to prior modeling work.

claim: Compte et al. (2000) showed that concomitant increase of NMDAR- and GABAR-mediated currents enhances resistance of the network to distractors.
source: In one seminal study by Compte et al., 2000, the authors investigated the robustness of working memory storage against external synaptic noise and distraction stimuli in attractor networks. They showed that a concomitant increase of NMDAR- and GABAR-mediated currents leads to an increase of persistent activity and to a decrease of spontaneous activity, thereby enhancing the resistance of the network to distractors (Brunel and Wang, 2001; Compte et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a reference to prior modeling work.

claim: Murray et al. (2014) demonstrated that disinhibition resulted in broadening of stimulus selective persistent activity and loss of precision.
source: In another prominent work, Murray et al., 2014, employing an attractor network model, investigated the neural and behavioral effects of synaptic disinhibition induced by the malfunction of NMDAR mediated synapses targeting inhibitory neurons. They demonstrated that disinhibition resulted in a broadening of stimulus selective persistent activity at the neural level, with a concomitant loss of precision, increase in variability over time, and increase in distractibility of stored information at the behavioral level.
evidence: This is a reference to prior modeling work.

claim: Prior modeling studies of working memory do not address how slow NMDAR recurrent excitation and external input jointly influence spike timing and oscillatory dynamics.
source: Although these modeling studies provide important mechanistic insight into prefrontal network dynamics underlying working memory, and potentially, working memory deficits in schizophrenia (Goldman-Rakic, 1999), they do not address the topic of the current study, which is how slow NMDAR recurrent excitation and external input received by the network jointly influence spike timing dynamics at the neuron level and oscillatory dynamics at the population level in the presence of fast AMPA excitation and GABA inhibition.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current work relative to prior studies.

claim: No prior modeling study captures the relationship between NMDAR synaptic mechanisms, spike timing, and network oscillations observed in neural recordings.
source: Thus, no prior modeling study captures the relationship between NMDAR synaptic mechanisms, spike timing, and network oscillations that we have observed in neural recordings (Kummerfeld et al., 2020; Zick et al., 2018), and for which we provide a theoretical explanation in the current report.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty and contribution of the current work.

claim: Reduced synchrony at the level of spiking neurons could disconnect prefrontal local circuits via spike-timing dependent synaptic plasticity.
source: We previously hypothesized that reduced synchrony at the level of spiking neurons (Zick et al., 2022; Zick et al., 2018) could disconnect prefrontal local circuits via spike-timing dependent synaptic plasticity (STDP; Dan and Poo, 2004; Feldman, 2012), contributing to the reduction in dendritic spine density that has been observed in postmortem analysis of prefrontal cortex in schizophrenia (Glantz and Lewis, 2000; MacDonald et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their prior work.

claim: Reduction in dendritic spine density has been observed in postmortem analysis of prefrontal cortex in schizophrenia.
source: We previously hypothesized that reduced synchrony at the level of spiking neurons (Zick et al., 2022; Zick et al., 2018) could disconnect prefrontal local circuits via spike-timing dependent synaptic plasticity (STDP; Dan and Poo, 2004; Feldman, 2012), contributing to the reduction in dendritic spine density that has been observed in postmortem analysis of prefrontal cortex in schizophrenia (Glantz and Lewis, 2000; MacDonald et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a reference to prior experimental observations.

claim: Prior theoretical studies incorporating STDP into spiking networks have obtained divergent results regarding how STDP changes synaptic connection patterns.
source: Perhaps for this reason, prior theoretical studies incorporating STDP into spiking networks have obtained divergent results with respect to how STDP changes the pattern of synaptic connections between neurons in networks, and whether synchronous inputs to the neurons are required for STDP to influence the pattern of synaptic connections.
evidence: This is a summary of prior theoretical work on STDP.

claim: STDP operating on random spiking can lead to formation of structured stable connections in the absence of synchronous inputs, depending on model assumptions.
source: For example, STDP operating on random spiking in neurons can either lead to the formation of structured stable connections between neurons in the absence of synchronous inputs (forming neural 'groups') (Izhikevich et al., 2004), or not (Morrison et al., 2007), depending on the assumptions incorporated into the models.
evidence: This is a reference to prior modeling work on STDP.

claim: Correlated external input to recurrent networks incorporating STDP can either fail to produce structured synaptic connections or lead to their formation, depending on simulation specifics.
source: Similarly, correlated external input to recurrent networks incorporating STDP can either fail to produce structured synaptic connections between neurons (Morrison et al., 2007), or it can lead to the formation of such structured connections (Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014) depending on the specifics of the simulations.
evidence: This is a reference to prior modeling work on STDP.

claim: Key parameters influencing diversity of STDP outcomes include whether axonal conduction delays and circuit geometry are incorporated, and the specific form of the STDP rule.
source: Key parameters that could influence the diversity of outcomes among studies include whether (Izhikevich et al., 2004) or not (Morrison et al., 2007) axonal conduction delays and the geometry of recurrent connections are incorporated into the models (since circuit architecture and associated signal conduction delays powerfully influences when action potentials arrive at pre- and postsynaptic elements), as well as the specific form of the STDP rule employed (Babadi and Abbott, 2013; Bono and Clopath, 2017; Izhikevich et al., 2004; Morrison et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a summary of factors affecting STDP modeling outcomes based on prior work.

claim: It seems reasonable that distortions of spike timing dynamics in prefrontal networks may alter the pattern of neural connections via STDP in schizophrenia.
source: Based on these results, it seems reasonable that distortions of spike timing dynamics in prefrontal networks may alter the pattern of neural connections via STDP in schizophrenia.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the review of prior STDP modeling work.

claim: The diversity of STDP modeling results makes it difficult to conclude that reduction in synchronous spiking would lead to synaptic disconnection via STDP.
source: However, the diversity of results obtained from theoretical studies of STDP outlined above make it difficult to conclude that the reduction in synchronous spiking we observed would lead to synaptic disconnection via STDP, imposing important constraints on our prior hypothesis (Zick et al., 2022; Zick et al., 2018), although this remains a possibility.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the authors' prior hypothesis based on the review of STDP literature.

claim: Genetic linkage studies have implicated altered NMDAR function in schizophrenia.
source: In addition, as noted, genetic linkage studies have implicated altered NMDAR function in schizophrenia (Fromer et al., 2014; Schizophrenia Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2014).
evidence: This is a reference to prior genetic studies.

claim: NMDAR play a central role in the molecular mechanisms that implement STDP in the brain.
source: Since NMDAR play a central role in the molecular mechanisms that implement STDP in the brain, disruption of NMDAR synaptic transmission in schizophrenia may alter STDP directly, independently of the impact of disrupted NMDAR function on neural spiking dynamics in the disease state.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about NMDAR and STDP.

claim: Disruption of NMDAR synaptic transmission in schizophrenia may alter STDP directly, independently of impacts on neural spiking dynamics.
source: Since NMDAR play a central role in the molecular mechanisms that implement STDP in the brain, disruption of NMDAR synaptic transmission in schizophrenia may alter STDP directly, independently of the impact of disrupted NMDAR function on neural spiking dynamics in the disease state.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms in schizophrenia.

claim: Blocking NMDAR in monkeys and deleting Dgcr8 in mice both reduced the frequency of synchronous, 0-lag spiking between prefrontal neurons.
source: We had previously reported that blocking NMDAR in monkeys (Zick et al., 2018) and deleting a schizophrenia risk gene (Dgcr8) in mice (Zick et al., 2022), both reduced the frequency of synchronous, 0-lag spiking between prefrontal neurons.
evidence: This is a reference to prior experimental work by the authors.

claim: Dgcr8 encodes a protein involved in the synthesis of miRNA.
source: Dgcr8 encodes a protein involved in the synthesis of miRNA, which in turn bind to mRNA and suppress their translation into proteins, including mRNA coding for NMDAR subunits (Corbel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a reference to prior molecular biology research.

claim: Deleting Dgcr8 would be expected to reduce miRNA synthesis and increase translation of mRNA coding for NMDAR subunits.
source: Deleting Dgcr8 would therefore be expected to reduce miRNA synthesis and increase translation of mRNA coding for NMDAR subunits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular function of Dgcr8.

claim: The convergent spike desynchronization in monkey drug and mouse genetic models could be explained by an inverted U-shaped relationship between NMDAR function and 0-lag spiking.
source: Given these considerations, the convergent spike desynchronization we observed in monkey drug and mouse genetic models could be explained by an inverted U-shaped relationship wherein either too little NMDAR function (as produced by NMDAR blockade in monkeys) or too much NMDAR function (as predicted to result from deletion of Dgcr8 in mice) decreases the frequency of 0-lag spiking between prefrontal neurons (Zick et al., 2022; Zick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain their experimental observations.

claim: An inverted U-shaped relationship has been reported between D1 dopamine receptor stimulation and persistent neural activity strength in prefrontal neurons.
source: An inverted U-shaped relationship has been reported between the level of D1 dopamine receptor stimulation and the strength of persistent neural activity in prefrontal neurons during working memory tasks wherein small doses of an agonist amplify persistent activity, and larger doses degrade it (Vijayraghavan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a reference to prior experimental work.

claim: Additional experimental data are needed to establish that spike synchrony exhibits an inverted U-shaped relation to NMDAR function.
source: However, additional experimental data are needed to establish that spike synchrony exhibits a similar inverted U-shaped relation to NMDAR function, insofar as our prior neural recording studies did not test a U-shaped relationship directly (Zick et al., 2022; Zick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior experimental work and the need for future studies.

claim: The current study establishes a theoretical basis and circuit mechanism explaining how reduction of NMDAR synaptic function could lead to desynchronization of neural activity in prefrontal recurrent circuits.
source: Results we present in the current study establish a theoretical basis and circuit mechanism explaining how reduction of NMDAR synaptic function implicated in schizophrenia could lead to the desynchronization of neural activity in prefrontal recurrent circuits.
evidence: This is a summary of the main contribution of the current study.

claim: Spiking networks situated close to a boundary in synaptic parameter space separating asynchronous and synchronous activity states can explain a variety of biological observations.
source: We provide evidence that spiking networks situated close to a boundary in the synaptic parameter space separating asynchronous and synchronous activity states can explain a variety of biological observations.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: The network model explains emergence of 0-lag synchronous spiking when external inputs push the network across the state boundary.
source: These include the emergence of 0-lag synchronous spiking between individual prefrontal neurons when external inputs to the network push it across this state boundary, and failure of synchronous spiking to emerge between prefrontal neurons when NMDAR synaptic currents are reduced, as we have observed in neural recordings in primate prefrontal cortex (Kummerfeld et al., 2020; Zick et al., 2022; Zick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary of how the model explains experimental observations.

claim: The network model explains failure of synchronous spiking to emerge when NMDAR synaptic currents are reduced.
source: These include the emergence of 0-lag synchronous spiking between individual prefrontal neurons when external inputs to the network push it across this state boundary, and failure of synchronous spiking to emerge between prefrontal neurons when NMDAR synaptic currents are reduced, as we have observed in neural recordings in primate prefrontal cortex (Kummerfeld et al., 2020; Zick et al., 2022; Zick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary of how the model explains experimental observations.
